say.text: Last segment. You rebuild TOF from memory and I only check it. Gate one: the backbone.
Which set lists the four components of classic TOF?

choices.label: VSD, overriding aorta, pulmonary stenosis, atrial septal defect
VSD, overriding aorta, RVOT obstruction, right ventricular hypertrophy
VSD, overriding aorta, RVOT obstruction, left ventricular hypertrophy

say.text: Think of the hole, the aorta's position, the outflow narrowing and the one chamber that works against it. No second shunt, no left side.
Yes. A large anteriorly malaligned VSD, an overriding aorta, infundibular RVOT obstruction and right ventricular hypertrophy.
That came from memory, so we skip the rebuild.
An ASD is tempting because it is a familiar extra hole, and old PYQs keyed PDA, ASD and LVH as 'not part of TOF'.
ASD and PDA may accompany TOF, but the four components include no ASD, PDA or LVH. The fourth is right ventricular hypertrophy.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so look twice: an accompanying lesion is not one of the four.

say.text: LVH is tempting because 'ventricular hypertrophy' does not name a side.
The thick ventricle in TOF is the right one, secondary to chronic systemic pressures, and the four include no LVH.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the side: it is the right ventricle that thickens.

say.text: Rebuild it as a chain. The anteriorly malaligned VSD sits with an overriding aorta, and the outflow narrows at the infundibulum.
The right ventricle then works against that narrowing under systemic pressure and thickens. RVH is the last link, secondary.
Same idea, new angle. Of the four components, which one develops as a consequence of the others?
Yes. The ventricle thickens because it pumps against the obstruction; RVH is secondary to chronic systemic pressures.
It is tempting to think a thick RV causes the narrowing, because the two are seen together.
The direction runs the other way. The infundibular obstruction is a component of the malformation; RVH is secondary to chronic systemic pressures.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so reverse the arrow: obstruction first, hypertrophy after.

say.text: The overriding aorta is tempting if you hold the four as a list with no cause and effect.
It belongs with the anteriorly malaligned VSD in the malformation itself. The secondary one is right ventricular hypertrophy.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so link it to the septum: the aorta overrides the malaligned VSD.

say.text: Gate two. A TOF chest X-ray: predict the lung fields from where the blood goes.

choices.label: Plethoric, because the VSD floods the lungs
Oligaemic, because blood bypasses the pulmonary bed

say.text: Ask where the blood goes when the way to the lungs is narrowed. Does more or less reach the lungs, and how big is the heart?
Yes. With significant RVOT obstruction most blood shunts toward the aorta, bypassing the lungs, so pulmonary markings are decreased.
Plethora is tempting because a VSD is a shunt and shunts often flood the lungs.
Here the obstruction sends blood toward the aorta, bypassing the pulmonary bed, so markings are decreased (oligaemia).

choices.label: Walk me through the film and ECG

sure_note.text: You were sure, so follow the blood: it bypasses the lungs.

say.text: Cardiomegaly is tempting because a thick ventricle sounds like a big heart.
StatPearls describes a normal-size heart silhouette with an upturned apex. The lung fields are oligaemic.

choices.label: Walk me through the film and ECG

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the size: normal silhouette, upturned apex.

say.text: Predict from the load. The RV pumps against the obstruction, so ECG shows right axis deviation and prominent R or qR waves in V1.
On film: oligaemic fields and a normal-size heart with an upturned apex. A 'boot' may classically be seen.
The ECG in TOF typically shows:

choices.label: Left axis deviation with an LVH pattern
Right axis deviation with an RVH pattern
Left atrial enlargement with an LVH pattern

say.text: Yes: right axis deviation, prominent R or qR in V1, upright T in V1, with right atrial enlargement and RVH.
Left-sided changes tempt when 'ventricular hypertrophy' is stored without a side.
The load is on the right ventricle, so the ECG shows right axis deviation and RVH.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so re-derive it: right ventricle loaded, right-sided ECG.

say.text: Left atrial enlargement tempts as the partner of left-sided hypertrophy.
The ECG describes right atrial enlargement and right ventricular hypertrophy, with right axis deviation.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the side: right atrium, right ventricle.

say.text: Gate three, cold: no hints. Which pairing of test and job is right in TOF?

choices.label: MRI for first-line diagnosis; echo only for later follow-up
Echo for diagnosis; MRI for anatomy plus function without radiation
Catheterisation as gold standard; echo only for early screening

say.text: Yes. Echo is the gold standard and primary diagnostic modality, and MRI adds anatomy and function without ionising radiation.
Contrast-enhanced CT is the other adjunct, useful for the complex morphology.
MRI is tempting because it gives anatomy and function without ionising radiation.
But echo remains the primary diagnostic modality because it directly visualises the abnormal anatomy. MRI is an adjunct.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so rank them: echo first, MRI as the extra.

say.text: Catheterisation is tempting because an invasive test feels more definitive.
The echocardiogram is the gold standard for diagnosis and remains the primary modality.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so reset the ladder: echo answers the diagnosis question.

say.text: Gate four. A 6-month-old with TOF goes into a tet spell. Which order is best?

choices.label: Phenylephrine, then morphine, then knee-chest and oxygen
Oxygen, then IV furosemide, then digoxin
Knee-chest and oxygen, then IV fluids, then beta-blocker or phenylephrine

say.text: Start with what you can do at the bedside in seconds. Then ask which later step aims to fill the right ventricle.
Yes. Knee-chest positioning, oxygen, IV fluid boluses, then IV beta-blockers or phenylephrine. Morphine can sedate.
Drugs first is tempting because they feel stronger than bedside measures.
The listed measures begin with knee-chest positioning and oxygen, then IV fluid boluses, IV beta-blockers and phenylephrine; morphine is a sedative. The approach is rapid and aggressive.

choices.label: Show me the lever behind it

sure_note.text: You were sure, so reorder it: bedside measures lead.

say.text: Furosemide and digoxin tempt when a blue, breathless child is filed under heart failure.
A spell calls for IV fluid boluses to improve RV filling and measures that increase systemic afterload, not volume removal.

choices.label: Show me the lever behind it

sure_note.text: You were sure, so drop the heart-failure reflex: fill the RV, raise afterload.

say.text: Cold check, no hints. Knee-chest positioning helps a child in a spell by:

choices.label: Reducing venous return to the right heart

say.text: Yes. Knee-chest positioning increases systemic vascular resistance. IV phenylephrine pulls the same lever by increasing systemic afterload.
Lowering pulmonary resistance is tempting because the aim is more lung flow, and oxygen does dilate the lungs.
Positioning works on the other side of the balance: it increases systemic vascular resistance.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so separate the levers: oxygen acts on the lungs, knee-chest on systemic resistance.

say.text: Reducing venous return tempts as the way to unload a struggling heart.
In a spell the RV needs filling: IV fluid boluses improve RV filling. Knee-chest increases systemic vascular resistance.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so recall the aim: fill the RV, raise systemic resistance.

say.text: Gate five. After TOF repair, the commonest reason for reoperation is:
Think about what the surgeon has to rebuild in the outflow tract, and what that rebuilt part can no longer do well.
Yes. Pulmonary regurgitation results from reconstruction of the RVOT, and pulmonary insufficiency is the most common indication for reoperation.
Replacement can be surgical or transcatheter.
A residual hole is tempting because you picture the original defects returning.
The repair itself creates the new problem: pulmonary regurgitation results from RVOT reconstruction, and pulmonary insufficiency is the commonest reoperation indication.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so shift the question: what does the repair cause?

say.text: Recurrent narrowing tempts because the first problem was an obstruction.
The commonest reoperation indication is pulmonary insufficiency, which follows RVOT reconstruction.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so recall the key: insufficiency, not stenosis.

say.text: Cold check, no hints. A 25-year-old had TOF repaired in infancy and asks about future risks. Which statement is true?

choices.label: Repair is curative, so arrhythmia risk has ended
Endocarditis risk ended with the repair
Ventricular arrhythmias and sudden death remain risks

say.text: Yes. Ventricular tachycardia can follow repair; 40-50% of adults with repaired TOF can have ventricular arrhythmias, and sudden death risk is 6-9% at 30 years.
Endocarditis risk applies to repaired or unrepaired TOF.
'Cured' is tempting because the anatomy has been fixed.
Arrhythmias including ventricular tachycardia can occur after repair: 40-50% of adults with repaired TOF can have ventricular arrhythmias, with 6-9% sudden death risk at 30 years.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so keep the qualifier: repaired still carries risk.

say.text: It is tempting to think a fixed defect removes the infection risk.
Patients with TOF, repaired or unrepaired, are at risk of endocarditis.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so reread the qualifier: repaired or unrepaired.

cards.a: Large anteriorly malaligned VSD, overriding aorta, infundibular RVOT obstruction, right ventricular hypertrophy. ASD and PDA may accompany it.

cards.q: Which TOF component is secondary, and to what?
cards.a: Right ventricular hypertrophy, secondary to chronic systemic pressures against the obstruction.
Oligaemic lungs, normal-size heart with upturned apex; ECG with right axis deviation and RVH pattern.

cards.q: Gold standard test for TOF diagnosis?
cards.a: Echocardiography; MRI adds anatomy and function without ionising radiation.

cards.q: Tet spell: order of steps and lever of knee-chest?
cards.a: Knee-chest (raises systemic resistance), oxygen, IV fluids, then IV beta-blocker or phenylephrine.

cards.q: Commonest reoperation indication after TOF repair?
cards.a: Pulmonary insufficiency, from RVOT reconstruction. Arrhythmia risk persists.
